title: Focusing Feedback on What Others Are Capable Of
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece warns leaders against giving feedback on qualities and skills that a team member is fundamentally incapable of changing. While good leaders naturally assess a broad range of attributes with an eye toward long-term development, the author distinguishes between genuine weaknesses that can improve and fixed traits — like being a highly strategic thinker or a polished public speaker — that some people will simply never possess. Judging people against standards they can't reach, the piece argues, is both discouraging and unproductive, sending them down dead ends instead of building on real strengths. The article closes with the well-known fish-climbing-a-tree analogy to underscore that feedback should target what someone is capable of changing, not an unreachable ideal.
points: Leaders often judge team members on qualities and skills they are fundamentally incapable of changing.
This differs from genuine, correctable weaknesses, which good leaders should continue to address.
Examples of largely fixed traits include being a visionary thinker, a polished public speaker, or highly resilient.
Giving feedback on unchangeable traits is both deflating and unproductive for the team member.
Good leaders concentrate assessment and feedback on what someone is realistically capable of improving.
quotes: Leaders are in the business of evaluating and judging others.
This makes perfect sense until leaders assess a feature the team member is entirely incapable of.
The truth is that some team members will never be highly strategic, visionary thinkers, or emotionally intelligent.
Judging people and giving them feedback on skills and qualities they are unable to achieve is both deflating and debilitating.
Good leaders know exactly what team members are capable of and concentrate their efforts on assessment and feedback that matters.
Everybody is a genius. But if you judge a fish by its ability to climb a tree, it will live its whole life believing that it is stupid.
